title: On the Existence of an Extremal Function for the Delsarte Extremal Problem

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Section 1 Introduction (vs. Theorems 8 and 9)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states that the paper shows existence of an extremal function 'when Ω is closed,' suggesting a general existence result for any closed Ω. However, the actual main theorems (Theorem 8 and Theorem 9) require Ω to be a 'closed neighbourhood of 0' (i.e., 0 ∈ int Ω). The paper itself notes earlier that if Ω is closed but not a neighbourhood of 0, the class 𝒢_G(Ω) is empty and hence no extremal function can exist at all. This makes the abstract's blanket claim about 'Ω closed' an overstatement relative to the actual, more restrictive hypothesis used in the proofs.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 1, paragraph beginning 'It may happen that the class 𝒢_G(Ω) is empty...'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text argues: 'if f is positive definite, then |f(g)| ≤ f(0) for all g ∈ G, and if 0 ∉ int Ω, then f(0) = 0, and hence f is identically 0.' The inequality |f(g)| ≤ f(0) by itself does not imply that f(0)=0 whenever 0 ∉ int Ω; this implication actually requires a continuity argument (continuity of f at 0 together with f(0)=1 would force a neighbourhood of 0 to lie in supp f_+, contradicting 0 ∉ int Ω). The stated justification is a non-sequitur as written, since the cited inequality is unrelated to the claimed conclusion about f(0).

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3, case '0 ∉ int Ω'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof states: 'Then, both 𝒢_G(Ω) and 𝒢_H(Ω) are empty. Therefore, both sides of (1) are equal to 0.' Under the standard mathematical convention, the supremum of an empty set is −∞ (or undefined), not 0. The paper never explicitly defines D_G(Ω) to equal 0 when the underlying class is empty, so this step relies on an unstated and non-standard convention, creating a mathematical inconsistency with the otherwise careful sup-based definition of D_G(Ω) given earlier in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract/Introduction definition of P_1(G) vs. Section 2 definition of P(G) and P_1(G)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In the abstract and introduction, P_1(G) is explicitly defined as 'the collection of continuous positive definite functions f : G → ℝ satisfying f(0) = 1' (real-valued). In Section 2, however, C(G) is defined as the space of continuous functions to the complex numbers, P(G) ⊂ C(G) is defined as the collection of continuous positive definite functions on G (without restricting to real-valued functions), and P_1(G) := {f ∈ P(G) : f(0) = 1} is defined analogously without reinstating the real-valued restriction. This creates an internal inconsistency about whether the functions under consideration throughout the paper are real- or complex-valued.
